claims.text: Oxidation resistance and material integrity in multiprincipal-element alloys are governed by the formation of protective oxide scales.
Protective oxide scales nucleate preferentially along grain boundaries.
Reactive elements segregated at grain boundaries enable self-healing oxide formation.
Self-healing oxide formation slows overall oxidation and material degradation.
Reactive-element concentration and distribution at grain boundaries can be varied through composition adjustment or thermomechanical processing.
Grain boundaries provide pathways for rapid diffusion.
Grain boundaries are preferential sites for oxide nucleation.
At high temperatures, reactive elements at grain boundaries diffuse outward.
Outward diffusion of grain-boundary reactive elements nucleates an adherent oxide scale.
The adherent oxide scale acts as a self-healing barrier that reduces bulk material degradation.
Non-optimal reactive-element diffusion or segregation produces non-protective oxide layers.
Non-protective oxide layers accelerate oxidation and loss of material integrity.
Engineering grain-boundary chemistry will produce more uniform and adherent protective oxide scales than in baseline samples.
Engineering grain-boundary chemistry will lower oxidation-associated mass gain relative to baseline samples.
Engineering grain-boundary chemistry will improve retained mechanical integrity relative to baseline samples.
Lower or non-optimized grain-boundary reactive-element concentrations will produce higher oxidation rates and greater degradation.
The proposed behavior is expected under sustained oxidizing exposure around 1000°C.
The proposed behavior may not apply at significantly lower temperatures or in non-oxidizing atmospheres.
The relative contributions of bulk diffusion and grain-boundary diffusion are uncertain.
A lack of statistically significant differences in oxide-scale quality, mass gain, or mechanical performance between modified and baseline samples would falsify the hypothesis.
